newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica's Nats set truth body new apology deadline.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica's Nats set truth body new apology deadline.

text.p: South Africa's truth commission said on Wednesday accusations of bias against it by the opposition National Party (Nats) were so serious it would respond only after a full meeting of all commissioners.

The Nats had set a deadline of noon (1000 GMT) on Wednesday for an unconditional apology from commission chairman Archbishop Desmond Tutu but agreed to extend this to June 20, the day after the commmission is due to meet.

The Nats, led by former president F.W. de Klerk, also want Tutu's deputy Alex Boraine to resign from the Truth and Reconciliation Commission on the grounds that he violated its charter to remain politically impartial.
The row between the Nats and the commission erupted last month when Tutu and Boraine accused de Klerk of failing to fully accept responsibility for human rights abuses during apartheid.

The Nats said Tutu and Boraine had effectively found them guilty of atrocities and began a boycott of commission activities. They threatened legal action on Monday unless Tutu apologised and Boraine quit.

In a letter to the Nats on Wednesday, commission lawyer Hanif Vally said that "in view of the serious nature of the demands" the commission would respond only after the matter had been fully discussed.
"A meeting of the commissioners is due to be held on June 19. Thereafter your letter will receive a reply," Vally said.

The row was fuelled on Tuesday when African National Congress Justice Minister Dullah Omar referred in parliament to the Nuremberg Trials as an alternative way of getting to the truth of the apartheid era.
He said any member of the apartheid government who failed to apply for amnesty and had been guilty of a crime would be fully prosecuted.
Sheila Camerer, spokeswoman for the Nats, described Omar's remarks as "totally uncalled for and shocking".
"They give the lie to the ANC's commitment to reconciliation," she said.
The ANC issued a statement on Wednesday describing the Nats' demands to the truth commission as "arrogant and contemptuous".
"The Nats have no moral authority to question the legitimacy and impartiality of the commission," the ANC said.
The Nats have accused the commission of treating the ANC with kid gloves in its probe of human rights abuses committed by the movement during its armed struggle against apartheid.
Tutu was patron of an ANC-aligned group during the 1980s.
